verdict.reasoning: Patient says, “recently I'm wheezy. Uh, I have feel like kind of short of breath” and when asked duration: “Mmm, two, three days. Yeah, quite recently.”

Dyspnea on exertion and sentence difficulty: “I also used to walk to work but recently I can't because … I feel like very short of breath and sometimes I feel like I can't even finish sentence”. Dry cough: to “Have you coughed any phlegm up?” patient replies “No.”

No SOB at rest: to “are you… short of breath when you're sitting still? Or just when you walk?” patient answers “Just walk… currently I feel well.” No nocturnal symptoms: to “Have you been woken up at night time at all?” patient answers “No, just daytime working.”

Reported fever: “I have a fever.” But temp: doctor asks, “Did you say you checked your temperature already?” patient: “Yes, I checked, I have fever.” Doctor: “Was it normal?” patient: “Yeah, yeah.” Doctor: “What was your temperature?” patient: “Uh, thirty seven, yeah.”

Unable to walk to work: “I also used to walk to work but recently I can't because … very short of breath.” Can climb stairs and feels well at rest: to “are you… short of breath when you're sitting still?” patient: “No… currently I feel well.” and to “Are you able to get up and down the stairs OK?” patient: “Yeah.”

No chest pain: “Any chest pain?” patient: “No chest pain, no.” No sputum/hemoptysis: “Have you coughed any phlegm up?” patient: “No.” and “Any… blood in there when you cough?” patient: “No, I don't think so.”

Childhood asthma: “Uh, yes, I had asthma. I also had, uh, hay fever and eczema.” Severity: “when you were a child how bad was your asthma?” patient: “Uh, it's quite bad.” Occasional hospitalizations: “did you ever have to go to hospital with it?” patient: “Yeah, sometimes.”
History of hay fever: “Uh, yes, I had asthma. I also had, uh, hay fever and eczema.” Later: “Any other medical problems?” patient: “Uh, I have, uh, hay fever as well.”
History of eczema: “Uh, yes, I had asthma. I also had, uh, hay fever and eczema.”

Use of salbutamol every few weeks and around exercise: “Um, I took salbutamol? Salbutamol? Yeah.” Doctor: “you normally take that do you?” patient: “Normally, yeah.” Doctor: “how often do you normally need it?” patient: “Every, every few weeks?” and “What about when you exercise normally, do you have to use medication? Uh, inhalers?” patient: “Yeah, yeah, a bit.”
No drug allergies: “And any allergies to medications?” patient: “No, no allergies.”

Never smoked: “Do you smoke?” patient: “No, I don't smoke.” Alcohol: “Do you drink any alcohol regularly?” patient: “Yeah, one glass.” ... “Every two or three days? Depends, yeah.” and specifies wine.

Living situation: “Who do you live with at home?” patient: “I live with my partner.” Employment and WFH sick leave: “what's your job, day-to-day?” patient: “Uh, I'm engineer.” and “I used to walk to work, but recently I, I work from home or sometimes I take sick leave, yeah.”
Temperature: doctor asks “What was your temperature?” patient: “Uh, thirty seven, yeah.”

Asthma flare and symptom cluster reflect transcript: 2–3 days of wheeze/SOB (“two, three days”; “I'm wheezy… short of breath”), exertional symptoms and no chest pain/sputum or nocturnal symptoms as per earlier supported facts hpi-001, hpi-002, hpi-005. Doctor states, “it sounds like you've had a flare up of your asthma.”

Possible allergic or viral trigger: doctor says, “it sounds like you've had a flare up of your asthma. It could be, um, triggered by, if there's more pollen around, or there may be, you may have a viral infection, causing it to get worse.”
Allergic rhinitis/hay fever and atopy including eczema: “I also had, uh, hay fever and eczema” and later “I have, uh, hay fever as well.”
Dose and frequency: “if you increase it so you're taking it two to four puffs, like, every four hours?” Context is salbutamol inhaler. Spacer is to be prescribed to use with MDI.
Pharmacist teaching: “a spacer to use your inhaler a bit more efficiently, which the pharmacist can show you how you use that when you pick it up.”
Spacer and peak flow meter: “I can prescribe you a peak flow meter… and a spacer to use your inhaler a bit more efficiently.”
Peak flow twice daily: “when you get the peak flow meter… if you can record a value first thing when you wake up… And in the evening over the next week.”
Safety-net: “if you get a high temperature or your wheezing is getting worse, you need to call us back straightaway so we can just advise you further with that.”

Review in ~1 week and possible controller therapy: “it will be a good idea when you're feeling better if we can arrange just a review… because we may need to start some other medication for you.” and “You could arrange a review in a week or so.” ICS is an example of controller; the transcript supports consideration of additional controller medication without naming ICS.
Regular antihistamine: “the other thing to do would be to take a regular antihistamine. Which you can get from the pharmacy, I can put a on your notes about what to take.”
